title: Brothers and sisters (Unitatis Redintegratio 3)
hookLine: other baptized Christians are rightly called brothers and sisters
tomorrow: does a shift at work count as part of a church's mission?

cards: A Baptist friend's youth group. A Lutheran cousin's confirmation. An Orthodox neighbor's Easter, sometimes on a different Sunday.
What's the right word for the Christians across a church divide? Inside the Catholic Church, two honest instincts answer differently.
Unitatis Redintegratio, the council's decree on ecumenism, lets both speak, in a single paragraph.

teach.h: INSTINCT ONE: DON'T BLUR THE LINES.
teach.b: The first instinct, at its best: don't blur the lines. The divisions are real, over teaching, sacraments and how a church is ordered, and love doesn't pretend otherwise. The decree agrees.
It calls the communion with other Christians imperfect, and it doesn't hide the differences. It even says that, in the old splits, people on both sides were often to blame.
The second instinct, at its best: start from what's shared.
Whoever believes in Christ and has been truly baptized, the decree says, is in a real communion with the Catholic Church, though an imperfect one.
Those born into other communities can't be charged with the sin of the separation.
Justified by faith in baptism, they belong to Christ, have a right to be called Christians, and are rightly accepted as brothers by the Catholic Church's own children.
The paragraph also names gifts found beyond the Church's visible boundaries: the written word of God, the life of grace, faith, hope and love, gifts of the Spirit.

teach.h: ONE LORD, ONE FAITH, ONE BAPTISM.
teach.b: Underneath sits Paul's line: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." So the decree keeps both: real differences, and a real family.
It chose a family word on purpose. Siblings can disagree out loud and still share a name. Other churches describe these relationships in their own terms.

how: Catholics take part in prayer services with other Christians, especially during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, and the Church recognizes baptism given in many other churches.

games.q: at Thanksgiving your Catholic aunt says "stress the differences" and your Methodist uncle says "stress what we share." what does the decree do?
o: sides with your aunt: the differences come first.
sides with your uncle: the differences don't matter.
keeps both: real differences, and a real family.
games.why: Unitatis Redintegratio 3 names imperfect communion and real differences, and still calls the baptized of other churches brothers, by right.

practice: Bring to mind a Christian from another church: a friend, a coworker, a relative. Write them a short message that asks for nothing back, the kind you'd send a brother or a sister. Send it, or just hold their name in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Brothers and sisters. Unitatis Redintegratio's family word for baptized Christians of other churches.

orig.note: Greek for brothers: the New Testament's word for fellow believers.

carryVoice: The line to keep: rightly called brothers, and sisters too, with the differences still on the table. Until next time.
